metadata.title: What's on a Card.
metadata.purpose: A viewer with no physics or coding background can name what a formula card holds (equations, knowns, outputs, applicability, pitfalls), explain why conditions travel with the formula, and say how the team builds and checks new cards.

beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer — the ask lands answered
beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on formula cards: the engine's library of physics it trusts. When the engine solves a problem, it never makes up a formula. Every equation it uses comes from a card that was written and checked ahead of time. So what's actually on a card?

props.command: What is a formula card in the physics engine, and what does one actually contain?
output: Equations, knowns, and what it solves for
When it applies, and the usual mistakes
Each card checked against known answers

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, what's on a card, using one real card. Second, why every card carries its own conditions and warnings. And third, how the team builds new cards against real problems, and where the library is still thin. No physics or coding background needed.

The answer up front. A formula card is a small, checked package. The equations, when they apply, what you need to know to use them, and the common mistakes. The engine can only solve what its cards cover. That's a limit. But it's also the guarantee: every answer traces back to a card that was checked against known answers.

beats.new_visual_element: the spring card, field by field
beats.narration_text: Here's a real one: spring energy to kinetic energy. It needs three knowns: the mass, the spring constant, and how far the spring is compressed. It solves for one thing: speed. Its equation says the spring's stored energy, one half k x squared, becomes the block's energy of motion, one half m v squared. The answer comes out in meters per second, and it must be positive.

The card also says when it applies: an ideal spring, on a frictionless surface, with all the stored energy turning into motion. When the engine uses this card, that condition is written into the solution as an assumption. So you see what had to be true, not just the answer. A two kilogram block, a five hundred newton per meter spring, compressed fifteen centimeters, leaves at about two point three seven meters per second.

beats.new_visual_element: the usual mistake travels with the formula
beats.narration_text: Every card also carries its pitfalls: the mistake people actually make. The wave card warns that the number in front of x is the wave number, not the wavelength. The wavelength is two pi divided by it. The kinematics card warns about forgetting that starts from rest means a starting speed of zero. The warning sits right next to the formula it's about.

beats.new_visual_element: eight cards, built against real answers
beats.narration_text: So how do new cards get made? Against real problems. When the team measured the library against the UGPhysics benchmark, vibrations and waves had one hundred seventy-nine problems, and zero cards. So they built eight, and checked each one against the benchmark's published answers. A wavelength of four centimeters. A wave speed of sixty centimeters per second. Escape velocity from the Moon, two point three seven kilometers per second. All matched.

Where it's still thin. In the team's own words, the library has footholds, not depth. Rigid body dynamics has one hundred eighty problems, and one card. And symbol names aren't separated by meaning yet. T means tension on one card, and period on two others. Today the right card still wins. But the team warns that as the library grows, a collision like that will eventually pick the wrong card.

beats.new_visual_element: a formula comes with its conditions
beats.narration_text: So here's the takeaway. A formula is only as good as the conditions that come with it. When an A.I. model gives you a formula, ask when it applies, and what mistake people usually make with it. If it can't tell you, don't trust the formula yet.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with any formula you're learning. It asks Claude to write you a formula card of your own.

props.command: Write a formula card for [formula]. Include: the equations; what each symbol means, with units; when it applies; which knowns I need; the most common student mistake; and one worked example with numbers I can check.
